text:
IN
THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Gichuru v. Smith,

2010 BCSC 234

Date: 20100224

Docket:
S123626

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Mokua Gichuru

Plaintiff

And

Howard Smith and Howard Smith
Personal Law Corporation,

both doing business as “Howard Smith
& Company”

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Bruce

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

In Person

Counsel for the Defendants:

D. Sorensen, L. Smith

Place and Date of Hearing:

New Westminster, B.C.

February 9, 2010

Place and Date of Judgment:

New Westminster, B.C.

February 24, 2010

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The plaintiff is a lawyer and a member of the
Law Society of British Columbia. He commenced an action against the defendants
for damages arising out of his termination from employment prior to the
completion of his articles. In addition, the plaintiff claimed the defendant,
Mr. Smith, breached the fiduciary duties owed to him as an articled student
when he prematurely terminated his employment. The relief claimed includes the
loss of earnings during the balance of his articles, compensation for delayed
entry to the legal profession, punitive damages, and special costs.

[
2
]

The defendants apply for orders pursuant to
Rules 18(6), 18(7), 19(24) and 57,
Rules of Court
, to strike out certain
portions of the plaintiff’s statement of claim as disclosing no reasonable
cause of action. In particular, the defendants argue that paragraphs 15 to 28
of the statement of claim disclose no cause of action and should be struck out
pursuant to Rule 19(24). The defendants also argue all claims against Mr.
Smith, in his personal capacity, should be dismissed under Rule 18(6) and Rule
19(24). Lastly, the defendants argue the plaintiff’s claim for punitive damages
should be struck because he has failed to plead material facts that, if
presumed true, could support such a claim.

[
3
]

The plaintiff opposes the relief sought by the
defendants. He argues that if there are deficiencies in the statement of claim,
the remedy is to amend it rather than strike out the offending paragraphs.

BACKGROUND

[
4
]

The plaintiff signed an articled student
agreement on January 24, 2002 designating Mr. Smith as his principal. This
agreement was also signed by Mr. Smith on the same date. Due to a citation by
the Law Society of British Columbia, it subsequently became apparent that Mr.
Smith could not act as a principal to an articled student during the relevant
period. As a consequence, Mr. Carmen Beuhler, a lawyer who shared office space
with Mr. Smith, agreed to act as the plaintiff’s principal. The plaintiff and
Mr. Beuhler subsequently entered into an articled student agreement, and while
neither party appears to have a copy of this agreement, there is no dispute as
to its terms.

[
5
]

The plaintiff worked out of Mr. Smith’s office
and it was Mr. Smith who directed his work and supervised his performance as an
articled student. Apart from the articled student agreement, there is no
evidence of a written employment agreement between the parties.

[
6
]

By letter dated April 30, 2002, Mr. Smith
terminated the plaintiff’s articles with his law firm on the ground that there
were personality conflicts between himself and the plaintiff and between the
plaintiff and his staff. Mr. Smith gave the plaintiff two weeks pay in lieu of
notice. Mr. Smith reported the plaintiff’s termination to the Law Society.

[
7
]

Thereafter the Law Society asked Mr. Smith to
provide the circumstances leading to the plaintiff’s termination because, as a
matter of policy, any unilateral dismissal of an articled student must be
referred to the credentials committee who address any competency concerns. By
letter dated May 29, 2002, Mr. Smith responded with a lengthy explanation for
his decision to terminate the plaintiff’s articles and indicated that Mr.
Beuhler concurred with his decision to terminate his law firm’s relationship
with the plaintiff. Mr. Smith did not suggest that the plaintiff was terminated
due to any concerns about his competency to practice law.  Mr. Smith was quite
confident that the plaintiff would be able to successfully complete his
articles with another type of law firm.

[
8
]

It was not until April 25, 2008, that the
plaintiff commenced an action in the Provincial Court of British Columbia,
Small Claims Division, under Action No. 13554, claiming that Mr. Smith had
wrongfully terminated his contract of employment with Howard Smith &
Company on April 30, 2002. His claim included an allegation that Mr. Smith
violated his fiduciary duties to the plaintiff arising out of the articled student
agreement. Although his claim for damages was stated to be $54,000, the
monetary jurisdiction of the Provincial Court required that the plaintiff
abandon any claim in excess of $25,000.

[
9
]

The matter came on for hearing before Judge Chen
of the Provincial Court in April 2009. Judge Chen heard evidence from the
plaintiff and considered an expert report with respect to damages for delayed
entry to the legal profession. Ultimately, at the continuation of the trial in
September 2009, Judge Chen permitted the plaintiff to make an application to
transfer the file to this court pursuant to Rule 7.1(1) of the
Small Claims
Act Rules
. Judge Chen granted the application on November 9, 2009 and
provided written reasons.

[
10
]

The plaintiff filed a statement of claim in this
court on November 17, 2009. He pleaded that Mr. Smith agreed to hire him as an
articled student on January 24, 2002 for a term “to last at least until April
11, 2003”. He pleaded that the defendants, Mr. Smith and his law corporation,
agreed to pay him $1,850 per month plus benefits. The plaintiff pleaded that he
commenced employment as an articled student with Howard Smith & Company on
March 7, 2002, articled to Mr. Beuhler, and that Mr. Smith unilaterally terminated
his employment on April 30, 2002. Lastly, the plaintiff pleaded that “at all
material times during the plaintiff’s period of articling with Howard Smith
& Company, Smith was the plaintiff’s effective principal.”  Thereafter the
statement of claim outlines the correspondence between the Law Society and Mr.
Smith, the hiring of new articled students by the defendant law corporation
after the plaintiff’s termination, the proceedings before the Provincial Court,
and the remedies sought.

[
11
]

On November 30, 2009 the defendants filed a
statement of defence. The defendants pleaded that the plaintiff was employed by
the defendant Law Corporation and not by Mr. Smith in his personal capacity.
The defendants denied any breach of contract or a breach of fiduciary duty.
They also denied the existence of any fiduciary duties to the plaintiff.
Lastly, they denied that the plaintiff suffered any form of damages or loss of
wages as a result of their actions.

[
12
]

Mr. Smith filed an affidavit in this proceeding
dated December 18, 2009. Paragraphs 6 to 12 of this affidavit state as follows:

6.         In or around January, 2002, I
wished to take on the Plaintiff as an articled student.

7.         Regrettably, I was under a
citation at the time when the Plaintiff was seeking articles, and as such, I
was prohibited from having an articled student.

8.         In order to enable the Plaintiff
to commence his articles, Mr. Carmen Beuhler, another lawyer with whom I shared
my office, took Mr. Gichuru on as an articled student. As such, Mr. Beuhler was
the principal to Mr. Gichuru.

9.         On or about January 28, 2002, Mr.
Gichuru commenced working as an articled student employed by Howard Smith
Personal Law Corporation with Mr. Carmen Beuhler as his principal. ...

10.       At no point did I contemplate that
the Articles Agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendants was an
agreement to provide compensation and employment for a guaranteed fixed period
of time. ...the Articles Agreement specifically contemplates that the agreement
can be terminated.

11.       Mr. Carmen Beuhler has passed away
since Mr. Gichuru was articled to him.

12.       During
his articles, Mr. Gichuru worked only for Howard Smith Personal Law Corporation
under my direction.

[
13
]

In addition, Mr. Smith deposed in paragraphs 16
to 18 of his affidavit dated December 18, 2009 as follows:

16.       All of my written correspondence
with the Law Society of British Columbia concerning the Plaintiff was read and
authorized by Mr. Carmen Beuhler.

17.       I cannot recall any occasion where
I acted arbitrarily, wrongfully, improperly or unreasonably in relation to the
Plaintiff.

18.       Further,
I do not recall treating the Plaintiff in a callous, high-handed or malicious
manner. At all times, I have been honest in my dealings with and concerning the
Plaintiff.

[
14
]

The plaintiff did not file an affidavit in
response to the defendants’ application. In or about April 2009 the Defendants
applied to adjourn the trial set down for three days in March 2010. The
plaintiff filed an affidavit in response to the adjournment application. This
application was ultimately granted and the trial was adjourned until July 27,
2010.

ARGUMENT

[
15
]

The defendants’ application seeks an order
striking the following paragraphs from the statement of claim:

15.       In or about April 2002, Steve
Yung, the Defendants’ previous articled student, completed the Professional
Legal Training Course and became eligible to be called to the Bar.

16.       In or about May 2002 Smith hired
Yung as a junior associate.

17.       In or about June 2002 Erick
Chapman graduated from the University of British Columbia Faculty of Law.

18.       Smith had promised to give Chapman
articles as Smith was personal friends with Chapman’s step-father.

19.       In or about June 2002 Smith hired
Chapman as an articled student with Howard Smith & Company.

20.       Yung and/or Chapman occupied the
Plaintiff’s previous office space.

21.       On or about April 25, 2008 the
Plaintiff served the Defendants with a Notice of Claim in Small Claims Court
Action No. C13554.

22.       On or about May 14, 2008 the
Defendants filed a Reply.

23.       Smith stated in the Reply that he
had terminated the Plaintiff’s employment before April 22, 2002.

24.       Smith further stated in the Reply
that the Plaintiff failed to disclose that he had a history of schizophrenia
and was/or had been having psychiatric treatment for the same.

25.       Smith caused significant delays of
the trial by not providing his true availability to the Judicial Case Manager.

26.       Despite repeated requests, Smith
failed to disclose any relevant documentation other than correspondence with
the Law Society that the Plaintiff already possessed.

27.       Smith did not withdraw the false
statement with respect to the date of termination of the Plaintiff’s employment
until the first day of trial, April 9, 2009.

28.       Smith
taunted the Plaintiff outside the court room on April 9, 2009.

[
16
]

The defendants seek to strike these paragraphs
pursuant to Rule 19(24) and Rule 18(6) and (7). With respect to paragraphs 15
to 20, the defendants argue that even if true, these statements concerning the
hiring decisions of the defendant Mr. Smith are irrelevant to the plaintiff’s
claim, could not have caused damage to him, and do not establish a cause of
action.

[
17
]

In regard to paragraphs 21 to 28 of the
statement of claim, the defendants argue that the statements concerning the
proceedings in Small Claims Court, even if true, do not establish a cause of
action and do not support a claim for damages.

[
18
]

In support of their application to strike these
pleadings, the defendants rely upon
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian
Jewish Congress
(1999),
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266, 91 A.C.W.S. (3d) 362
(B.C.S.C.) [
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
cited to C.P.C.],
Lund v.
Black Press Group Ltd.
,
2007 BCSC 559
, 42 C.P.C. (6th) 349,
Canadian Bar
Association v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92 (CanLII)
, 2008 B.C.C.A. 92, 290 D.L.R. (4th) 617 [
Canadian
Bar Association
],
Freshway Specialty Foods Inc. v. Map Produce LLC
,

2005 BCSC 1485 (CanLII)
, 2005 B.C.S.C. 1485, 143 A.C.W.S. (3d) 668, and
Carnahan v. Coates

(1990),
1990 CanLII 2299 (BC SC)
, 71 D.L.R. (4th) 464, 47 B.C.L.R. (2d) 127 (S.C.) [
Carnahan
cited
to D.L.R.].

[
19
]

The defendants also argue that the claim for
punitive damages must be struck because there is no evidence to contradict Mr.
Smith’s sworn statement that there are no facts to justify such an award and,
in particular, no arbitrary, wrongful, improper, or unreasonable conduct on the
part of the defendants. In support of their submission, the defendants rely
upon
Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co.
,
2002 SCC 18 (CanLII)
, 2002 S.C.C. 18, [2002] 1 S.C.R. 595
[
Whiten
], and
Marchen v. Dams Ford Lincoln Sales Ltd.
,
2010 BCCA
29
, [2010] B.C.J. No. 86 [
Marchen
].

[
20
]

Further, the defendants argue that even if every
fact contained in the statement of claim were assumed to be true, a claim for
punitive damages would have no chance of succeeding. In particular, the
plaintiff does not allege high-handed, malicious, arbitrary, or highly
reprehensible misconduct that departs to a marked degree from ordinary
standards of decent behaviour. The defendants also argue the pleadings do not
disclose an actionable wrong causing injury to the plaintiff which could form
the basis for an award of punitive damages.

[
21
]

The defendants argue the plaintiff’s claim for
breach of fiduciary duty cannot proceed against the defendants. Mr. Smith was
not the plaintiff’s principal. The articled student agreement signed by Mr.
Smith was void for illegality or was superseded by the articled student
agreement between the plaintiff and Mr. Beuhler. In addition, Mr. Smith’s sworn
statement that there are no facts to support a claim for breach of fiduciary
duties is not contradicted by the plaintiff. The defendants argue the plaintiff
has not properly pleaded a breach of fiduciary duty because the pleadings lack
particulars of the special relationship, the duty of loyalty owed, the
vulnerability of the plaintiff, and the breach of the duty alleged. In support
of their position, the defendants rely upon
Immocreek Corp. v. Pretiosa
Enterprises Ltd.
(2000),
2000 CanLII 5703 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. (3d) 169, 186 D.L.R. (4th) 311 (C.A.) [
Immocreek
Corp.
].

[
22
]

Lastly, the defendants argue that the defendant,
Mr. Smith, should be removed as a defendant because there is no cause of action
against him in his personal capacity.  In particular, the defendants argue
there was no breach of contract committed by Mr. Smith because the employment
contract was between the plaintiff and the defendant law corporation. The
articled student agreement signed by Mr. Smith is either void for illegality,
frustrated due to Mr. Smith’s Law Society citation, or replaced by the
agreement with Mr. Beuhler. In addition, the articled student agreement does
not address the terms of employment. In support of this argument, the
defendants rely upon
Vandekerhove v. Litchfield
(1993),
1993 CanLII 660 (BC SC)
, 103 D.L.R. (4th)
739, [1994] 1 W.W.R. 596 (B.C.S.C.),
Neider v. Carda of Peace River District
Ltd.
,
1972 CanLII 131 (SCC)
, [1972] S.C.R. 678, 25 D.L.R. (3d) 363,
Naylor Group Inc. v.
Ellis-Don Construction Ltd.
,

2001 SCC 58
, [2001] 2 S.C.R. 943, and
Focal
Properties Ltd. v. George Wimpey Canada Ltd.
(1977),
1975 CanLII 49 (ON CA)
, 14 O.R. (2d) 295, 73
D.L.R. (3d) 387 (C.A.).

[
23
]

The plaintiff argues that the breach of fiduciary
duty is based upon the fact that Mr. Smith was his
de facto
principal.
The plaintiff argues that Mr. Smith has admitted this relationship in his reply
to the plaintiff’s notice of claim in the Small Claims Court action. If there
is a deficiency in the manner in which the claim is pleaded, the court should
permit an amendment and not strike out the claim under Rule 19(24) or Rule
18(6). In support of this argument, the plaintiff relies upon
Allen v.
College of Dental Surgeons of British Columbia
,

2005 BCSC 842
, 32
C.C.L.T. (3d) 256,
Young v. McLellan
,
2005 BCCA 563
, 218 B.C.A.C. 195,
and
Ross v. British Columbia (Public Safety)
,
2009 BCSC 930
, [2009]
B.C.J. No. 1381.

[
24
]

In regard to paragraphs 15 to 20 of the
statement of claim, the plaintiff argues that these are material facts showing
that the underlying reasons for his dismissal from employment are contrary to
those given by Mr. Smith. Although the language used by the plaintiff may not
be entirely clear, he argues the court should permit him to amend the pleadings
rather than striking them out. The plaintiff says the intention behind the
language can be inferred from the pleadings and no sworn evidence need be filed
in support of the proposed amendment.

[
25
]

In regard to paragraphs 21 to 28, the plaintiff
says these are material facts underlying his claim for punitive damages and
special costs. The actions of Mr. Smith subsequent to the dismissal are
relevant to both costs and punitive damages. The fact that Mr. Smith made false
allegations about the plaintiff’s mental health supports both claims. While the
plaintiff has failed to plead that the statement in question was false, he
argues this error could be corrected by an amendment to the pleadings. In
support of this argument, the plaintiff relies upon
Marchen
.

[
26
]

Further, while he has not pleaded that the
dismissal was wrongful, the plaintiff argues this can be inferred from the
pleadings and, in any event, could be the subject of an amendment.

[
27
]

Lastly, the plaintiff argues that he has a
bona
fide
claim against Mr. Smith in his personal capacity even though the
contract of employment was with the personal law corporation. In this regard,
the plaintiff says the corporate veil should be pierced because Mr. Smith is
the sole operating mind of his law corporation. While the facts underlying this
cause of action are not pleaded in the statement of claim, the plaintiff argues
he should be permitted to amend the pleadings rather than submit to an order
striking them out due to this deficiency.

DECISION AND DISCUSSION

A. Relevant Legislation

[
28
]

Rule 19(24) provides the court with a discretion
to strike out or amend pleadings as follows:

19(24)  At any stage of a proceeding
the court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an
endorsement, pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it discloses no reasonable claim
or defence as the case may be,

(b)        it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious,

(c)        it may prejudice, embarrass or
delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the
process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
29
]

Rule 18(6) and 18(7) provide for summary judgment as
follows:

18(6) In an action in which an appearance
has been entered, the defendant may, on the ground there is no merit in the
whole or part of the claim, apply to the court for judgment on an affidavit
setting out the facts verifying the defendant's contention that there is no
merit in the whole or part of the claim and stating that the deponent knows of
no facts which would substantiate the whole or part of the claim.

18(7) On the
hearing of an application under subrule (6) the court may

(a)        dismiss the action,

(b)        make any order referred to in
subrule (2), or

(c)        grant
any other order it thinks just.

[
30
]

The discretion granted to the court under Rules
18(6) and 19(24) must be exercised fairly and judiciously and in accordance
with the objects of the Rules, which are set out in Rule 1(5): “to secure the
just, speedy, and inexpensive determination of every proceeding on its merits.”

[
31
]

Rule 19(24) has been interpreted and applied
consistently as requiring the defendant to prove that it is “plain and obvious”
the pleading sought to be struck discloses no reasonable cause of action and,
if there is any doubt about this, it should be resolved in favour of permitting
the pleading to stand. A good summary of the principles to be applied is found
in
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
at para. 34:

[34]      To
succeed on an application under Rule 19(24) (a) it must be established that it
is “plain and obvious” that the pleading discloses no reasonable cause of
action:
Hunt v. T & N plc
,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 (S.C.C.).  If there
is any doubt it should be resolved in favour of permitting the pleadings to
stand:
McGauley v. British
Columbia
(1989),
1989 CanLII 2809 (BC CA)
, 39 B.C.L.R. (2d) 223 (B.C. C.A.).
The court should proceed on the assumption that all the facts pled are true:
Helman v. Brown

(1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608 (B.C. C.A.). The only question then is whether
the facts disclose a cause of action:
Minnes v. Minnes
(1962),

1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
, 39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.);
McNaughton
v. Baker
(1988),
1988 CanLII 3036 (BC CA)
, 25 B.C.L.R. (2d) 17 (B.C. C.A.).
In other words, as long as the pleadings disclose a triable issue, either as it
exists, or as it may be amended, then the issue should go to trial. The mere
fact that the case is weak or not likely to succeed is no ground for striking
it out under the provisions of Rule 19(24):
Minnes,
supra.

[
32
]

In
Canadian Bar Association
, the Court of
Appeal confirmed that in an application to strike pleadings under Rule
19(24)(a), the court must assume the facts alleged in the pleadings are true.
The court’s inquiry does not involve a consideration of any evidence led by the
parties and the plaintiff’s case is taken at its highest: per Saunders J.A. at
para. 37.

[
33
]

In contrast to an application under Rule
19(24)(a), a party seeking summary judgment under Rule 18(6) may adduce
evidence to support its position that the action is bound to fail. Otherwise,
the legal principles to be applied are quite similar. As Huddart J. (as she
then was) says in
Carnahan

at 466:

An order for summary judgment can be granted
only if the plaintiffs are bound to lose. Matters of fact cannot be weighed.
Inferences from the facts must be viewed in the light most favourable to the
plaintiffs. In other words, the defendants are required to establish that there
is no
bona fide
triable issue of fact or law...

This test is
only slightly less stringent than that required under Rule 19(24). The Court of
Appeal upheld a decision in chambers that an earlier application by the
defendants under that rule was premature. The significant difference is that
evidence is available on this motion that could not be considered on the
earlier motion which was required to be decided on the pleadings.

[
34
]

A concise summary of the law regarding Rule
18(6) is also found in
Pitt v. Holt
,

2007 BCSC 1555
, 162 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 272 [
Pitt
], at para.
10
:

[10]      On an application under Rule
18(6), the court may make an order for summary judgment in favour of a
defendant dismissing an action only where a plaintiff is "bound to
lose". Another way of stating the test is whether there is a bona fide
triable issue to be determined:
Serup v. Board of Trustees of School
District #57
,
1989 CanLII 5192 (BC CA)
, 57 D.L.R. (4th) 261 at 264, 54 B.C.L.R. (2d) 258 (C.A.). In
Skybridge
Investments Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd. (c.o.b. Metro Ford
),
2006 BCCA 500
, 61
B.C.L.R. (4th) 241, Thackray J.A. at paras. 10-13 states, as follows:

A judge hearing an application pursuant to
Rule 18(6) must: examine the pleaded facts to determine which causes of action
they may support; identify the essential elements required to be proved at
trial in order to succeed on each cause of action; and determine if sufficient
material facts have been pleaded to support each element of a given cause of
action.

If
insufficient
material facts have
been pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, then beyond a doubt
that cause of action is bound to fail and a defendant bringing an application
pursuant to Rule 18(6) will have met the onus to negative the existence of a
bona
fide
triable issue.

If
sufficient
material facts have
been pleaded to support every element of a cause of action, but one or more of
those pleaded material facts are contested, then the judge ruling on a Rule
18(6) application is not to weigh the evidence to determine the issue of fact
for the purpose of the application. The judge's function is limited to a
determination as to whether a
bona fide
triable issue arises on the
material before the court in the context of the applicable law. If a judge ruling
on a Rule 18(6) application must assess and weigh the evidence to arrive at a
summary judgment, the "plain and obvious" or "beyond a
doubt" test has not been met.

On appeal, as on the application in
chambers, the question addressed in a Rule 18(6) application of whether there
is a
bona fide
issue to be tried must be decided assuming that the
uncontested material facts as pleaded by the plaintiff are true:
Van Den
Akker v. Naudi,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 1649, 1997 CarswellBC 1470 (B.C.C.A.)
.

B. Application to Strike Paragraphs
15 to 28 of the Statement of Claim.

[
35
]

Turning to the defendants’ application to strike
paragraphs 15 to 20 of the statement of claim under Rule 19(24), it is
difficult to determine the reasoning behind the plaintiff’s decision to include
these facts as part of his claim for breach of fiduciary duties. Based on the
pleadings alone, there is no connection between the plaintiff’s dismissal as an
articled student and Mr. Smith’s decision to hire another articled student and
an associate. This is particularly evident when one considers that the
plaintiff has not specifically pleaded a wrongful dismissal or a breach of his
employment contract. Although the plaintiff has pleaded a breach of fiduciary
duties, the statement of claim does not particularize the basis for this claim
at all or in a way that would connect paragraphs 15 to 20 to this cause of
action.

[
36
]

The plaintiff argues that the court can infer
from paragraphs 15 to 20 that Mr. Smith did not have a
bona fide
reason
for terminating his employment as an articled student. In particular, the
plaintiff says the language of the disputed paragraphs can be inferred to mean
that Mr. Smith terminated his employment to hire these other persons. This
inference would have been less difficult to draw had the plaintiff articulated
the nature of Mr. Smith’s breach of fiduciary duties or had he pleaded a breach
of the employment contract or wrongful dismissal. Nevertheless, the authorities
clearly indicate that if the pleadings show a triable issue, as framed or as
may be amended, they should not be struck. In my view, these paragraphs could
conceivably disclose a cause of action if pleaded in conjunction with the claim
for breach of fiduciary duties; that is, Mr. Smith breached the fiduciary
duties owing to the plaintiff by terminating his employment as an articled
student for the purpose of hiring another articled student and an associate. A
party should generally be permitted to amend pleadings in response to an
application to strike under Rule 19(24) if, as amended, they raise a triable
issue:
Helman v. Brown
(1966),
1966 CanLII 597 (BC CA)
, 57 W.W.R. 608, [1966] B.C.J. No. 48
(C.A.).

[
37
]

Addressing the defendants’ application to strike
paragraphs 21 to 28 of the statement of claim, I find these pleadings disclose
a triable issue in respect of the plaintiff’s claim for special costs. In
Marchen
,
the Court of Appeal confirmed the well established principle that special costs
are awarded for the conduct of parties leading up to and in the course of
litigation: per Chiasson J. A. at para. 69. The nature of the conduct
attracting an order of special costs has been characterized by the authorities
as “reprehensible”. In
Stanton v. Stanton Estates
,
2008 BCCA 362
, 43
E.T.R. (3d) 1, the Court of Appeal adopted the reasoning of Madam Justice Strongberg-Stein
(in Chambers) in
Benekritis v. Benekritis Estate,

77 A.C.W.S. (3d) 227,
[1998] B.C.J. No. 171 [
Benekritis
cited to QL]
, concerning when special
costs will be awarded. The relevant passages in
Benekritis
are at para.
54:

[54]      The court may order special costs
under R. 57(3). In Garcia v. Crestbrook Forest Industries Ltd.

(1994),

1994 CanLII 2570 (BC CA)
, 14 C.C.E.L. (2d 84 (B.C.C.A.) at 91, the Court found the “single standard for
the awarding of special costs is that the conduct in question properly be
characterized as ‘reprehensible’”. The Court went on, at 91, to describe the
wide meaning that is attributed to the word “reprehensible”:

...the word reprehensible is a word of
wide meaning. It encompasses scandalous or outrageous conduct but it also
encompasses milder forms of misconduct deserving of reproof or rebuke.
Accordingly, the standard represented by the word reprehensible, taken in that
sense, must represent a general and all-encompassing expression of the
applicable standard of the award of special costs.

[
38
]

Paragraphs 21 to 28 of the statement of claim
clearly relate to the defendants’ actions leading up to and during the
litigation. Further, it is conceivable that some of the alleged misconduct, if
true, may be worthy of rebuke. While the facts pleaded in the plaintiff’s
statement of claim may show only a weak case or little likelihood of
succeeding, this is not a ground for striking the pleadings under Rule 19(24)
or granting summary judgment under Rule 18(6). Thus I must dismiss this portion
of the defendants’ application.

C. Application to Strike or Dismiss
the Claim for Punitive Damages

[
39
]

Punitive damages are a remedy for egregious
conduct of a defendant at the time of the alleged breach giving rise to the
cause of action. In
Marchen
, the Court of Appeal discussed the basis for
an award of punitive damages in paras. 66 and 67:

[66]      Punitive damages are awarded to
express approbation and to punish in circumstances where the global amount of
damages awarded, including aggravated damages in appropriate circumstances, is
insufficient (
Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co
.,
2002 SCC 18
, [2002] 1
S.C.R. 595 at para.
94
; B.P.B. v. M.M.B.,
2009 BCCA 365
at para.
59
).
...

[67]      In
breach of contract cases, punitive damages flow out of egregious conduct of a
defendant at the time of the breach. In this case, when dismissing the claim
for moral damages, the judge held that the appellant’s “conduct at the time of
termination was not unfair, unfaithful, misleading or unduly insensitive.” He
also held that Mr. Marchen did not suffer undue distress. On these findings of
fact, punitive damages are not available.

[
40
]

In
Whiten

at para.
78
, Binnie J. (writing
for the majority) concluded that in a breach of contract claim the plaintiff
must prove that the blameworthy conduct giving rise to punitive damages
constituted an actionable wrong independent of the breach of contract. Binnie
J. also held that punitive damages are, “imposed only if there has been
high-handed, malicious, arbitrary or highly reprehensible misconduct that
departs to a marked degree from ordinary standards of decent behaviour.” (at
para. 94).

[
41
]

There are no facts pleaded in the statement of
claim that, if true, could establish a claim for punitive damages based on the
standard articulated in the authorities cited above. The plaintiff alleges no
conduct at the time of the breach that could be characterized as high-handed,
malicious, arbitrary or highly reprehensible. Moreover, in support of the
defendants’ application under Rule 18(6) for summary judgment, Mr. Smith
deposed that he could not recall any occasion where he “acted arbitrarily,
wrongfully, improperly or unreasonably in regard to the plaintiff” and,
further, “he could not recall any occasion that he treated the plaintiff in a
callous, high-handed or malicious manner”. The plaintiff did not file affidavit
evidence to contradict these sworn statements by Mr. Smith.

[
42
]

Accordingly, I find that the defendants are
entitled to an order under Rule 18(7) dismissing this part of the plaintiff’s
claim.

D. Application to Strike or Dismiss
the Plaintiff’s Action as against Mr. Smith

[
43
]

Insofar as it may be inferred that the plaintiff
is suing in contract for a breach of his employment contract, any claim against
Mr. Smith in his personal capacity must be dismissed under Rule 18(6) or the
pleading struck under Rule 19(24). The plaintiff admits that he was employed by
the defendant, Howard Smith & Company. The plaintiff does not allege a
contract of employment with Mr. Smith in his personal capacity. Further, the
plaintiff has not pleaded any basis for concluding that Mr. Smith, in his
personal capacity, had a separate identity or interest from the corporate
defendant in the employment contract. In addition, the plaintiff admits that he
was articled to Mr. Beuhler rather than to Mr. Smith. Thus there is no
contractual relationship between the plaintiff and Mr. Smith stemming from the
articled student agreement that could support a claim based upon breach of
contract. Further, and in any event, it is apparent that the original articled
student agreement wherein Mr. Smith agreed to act as the plaintiff’s principal
was either void for illegality or superseded by the subsequent articled student
agreement signed by Mr. Beuhler.

[
44
]

During his submissions, the plaintiff asserted a
claim against Mr. Smith, in his personal capacity, on the ground that he is the
sole operating mind of the law corporation. The plaintiff failed to plead this
material fact and did not file an affidavit in these proceedings attesting to
this fact. Thus the court is not entitled to consider the plaintiff’s bare
assertion as a ground for dismissing the defendants’ application to strike the
pleading. However, even if this fact was pleaded, I find it is insufficient to
support a claim against Mr. Smith in his personal capacity. The officers,
directors and employees of a limited company are protected from personal
liability except in a very limited category of cases. The circumstances in
which the court will lift the corporate veil to render an officer or director
personally liable are described by the Ontario Court of Appeal in
Montreal
Trust Co. of Canada v. ScotiaMcLeod Inc.
(1995),
1995 CanLII 1301 (ON CA)
, 26 O.R. (3d) 481, 129
D.L.R. (4th) 711 at 720:

The decided
cases in which employees and officers of companies have been found personally
liable for actions ostensibly carried out under a corporate name are
fact-specific. In the absence of findings of fraud, deceit, dishonesty or want of
authority on the part of employees or officers, they are also rare. Those cases
in which the corporate veil has been pierced usually involve transactions where
the use of the corporate structure was a sham from the outset or was an
afterthought to a deal which had gone sour. There is also a considerable body
of case law wherein injured parties to actions for breach of contract have
attempted to extend liability to the principals of the company by pleading that
the principals were privy to the tort of inducing breach of contract between
the company and the plaintiff: see
Ontario Store Fixtures Inc. v. Mmmuffins
Inc
. (1989),
1989 CanLII 4229 (ON HCJ)
, 70 O.R. (2d) 42 (H.C.J.), and the cases referred to therein.
Additionally there have been attempts by injured parties to attach liability to
the principals of failed businesses through insolvency litigation. In every
case, however, the facts giving rise to personal liability were specifically
pleaded. Absent allegations which fit within the categories described above,
officers or employees of limited companies are protected from personal
liability unless it can be shown that their actions are themselves tortious or
exhibit a separate identity or interest from that of the company so as to make
the act or conduct complained of their own.

[
45
]

This decision was cited with approval in
607730
B.C. Ltd. v. Quay Realty Investments Ltd.
,
2009 BCCA 575
, [2009] B.C.J. No.
2697, at para.
11
.

[
46
]

None of these circumstances are present in the
case at hand. The mere fact that Mr. Smith is the sole principal of his law
corporation does not provide a proper basis for piercing the corporate veil. I
thus grant the defendants’ application to dismiss any claim for breach of
contract against Mr. Smith in his personal capacity pursuant to Rule 18(6) and
(7).

[
47
]

Lastly, the defendants argue that the claim
against Mr. Smith for breach of fiduciary duty should be struck either under
Rule 19(24) of Rule 18(6). The defendants argue there is no relationship
between Mr. Smith and the plaintiff giving rise to fiduciary duties. The only
party to a claim arising out of an alleged fiduciary relationship between
articled student and principal would be Mr. Beuhler.  In my view, this portion
of the defendants’ application must be dismissed because it is not plain and
obvious that the plaintiff’s pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action
or is bound to fail. While the pleadings are clearly deficient, they may be
amended to correct the deficiencies.

[
48
]

As I interpret the plaintiff’s statement of
claim, he alleges that a fiduciary relationship existed between himself and Mr.
Smith as his
de facto
principal. Mr. Smith acknowledges in his affidavit
dated December 18, 2009, that during the plaintiff’s articles the plaintiff
only worked for his law corporation and under his direction. Further, by
implication, the plaintiff claims the abrupt termination of the articled
student relationship violated the fiduciary duties owed to him by Mr. Smith. While
Mr. Smith deposes that he knows of no facts to support a claim for breach of
fiduciary duties, the statement of claim, when given the interpretation most
favourable to the plaintiff, contradicts this position. In particular,
paragraphs 15 to 20 appear to suggest the plaintiff was terminated to
facilitate the hiring of another articled student and, generally, the statement
of claim may be inferred to mean that any termination of an articled student
prior to completion of the articling year is a breach of the principal’s fiduciary
duties. The authorities are clear that in an application for summary judgment
under R. 18(6) a judge should not weigh the evidence to determine issues of
fact; the judge should only determine whether there is a
bona fide

triable issue on the material facts pleaded. Here, unlike the circumstances in
Immocreek
Corp.
,
at a minimum the plaintiff’s statement of claim pleads the necessary
facts for a claim based upon a breach of fiduciary duty by Mr. Smith.

[
49
]

Further, the authorities are clear that where a
pleading may be amended the offending party should be given an opportunity to
do so in preference to striking the claim or dismissing the action. The
plaintiff must amend his pleadings to clearly set out the breach of fiduciary
duty as a cause of action and to identify its legal components and the material
facts supporting the claim.

E. Conclusion

[
50
]

In summary, the plaintiff’s claim for punitive
damages is struck and the claim against Mr. Smith, in his personal capacity,
for breach of contract is dismissed. The balance of the defendants’ application
is dismissed.

[
51
]

My decision is based upon the plaintiff carrying
out the proper amendments to the statement of claim. In light of the delay in
this case, the plaintiff shall have fourteen (14) days from the date of this
judgment to file an amended statement of claim. Any failure to comply with this
time limit shall entitle the defendants to re-apply for dismissal on two (2)
days’ notice to the plaintiff.

[
52
]

The parties have had divided success in this
application; however, in my view, the defendants’ application was necessary due
to the woefully inadequate drafting of the statement of claim. The plaintiff is
self represented; however, he is a lawyer and a member of the Law Society of
British Columbia. As a consequence, there is a greater expectation placed on
him to prepare pleadings in compliance with the
Rules of Court
than on a
lay person. For these reasons, the plaintiff shall bear the defendants’ costs
of this application in any event of the cause. Pursuant to Rule 57(13.1), I
award lump sum costs in the amount of $1800, inclusive of disbursements. The
plaintiff shall not be entitled to file his amended statement of claim or take
any further step in the within action until he has paid these costs in full.

“Bruce
J.
”
